## Collaboration Note:

We were allowed to collaborate on these capstone projects if they aligned with both of our interests and could conceivably be a for a project that would benefit both of us. Looking at maternal mental health and child emergency department visits is a perfect alignment of our interests. Camille is a caregiving researcher whose primary interests revolve around the total-family impacts of illness. Korie is a maternal-child health researcher whose prior work has focused on veterans and how healthcare access for parents shifts childrens' health outcomes. After taking comprehensive exams in May, we plan to revisit this analysis and write it into a manuscript.

## Introduction and Significance

*Pediatric ED Use*

Emergency department (ED) utilization among children remains a persistent policy concern in the United States (US) healthcare system, particularly when visits might be avoided through timely preventive care, seeking appropriate level of care acuity (e.g., urgent care vs. ED), or better at-home management of conditions. Nearly 13% of pediatric ED visits are for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions that could likely be prevented or managed with timely primary care services (Jaeger et al., 2015). Numerous factors have already been identified to be associated with recurrent ED visits among children including being in a low-income household (\<200% Federal Poverty Level \[FPL\]), being publicly insured, and residing in neighborhoods with poor physical or social conditions (Chang et al., 2021; Jaeger et al., 2015). Thus, ED use among children signals gaps in primary care access or broader social inequities and contributes to healthcare costs and ED overcrowding, straining an already overburdened system (Chang et al., 2021; Neuman et al., 2014).

*Maternal Mental Health (MH) as a Driver of ED Use*

Growing evidence also suggests that maternal mental health (MH) is related to ED visits. Maternal depression and anxiety, along with other psychosocial risk factors, have been linked to increased ED use among infants and young children. Rokicki (2024) demonstrated that even mild perinatal depressive symptoms were associated with higher rates of both emergent and nonemergent ED visits during infants’ first year of life, especially among Medicaid-enrolled families (Rokicki, 2024). Similarly, Guyon-Harris et al. (2021) found that prenatal maternal MH symptoms, low relational health, and maternal histories of childhood maltreatment were significant predictors of increased infant ED utilization (Guyon-Harris et al., 2021). Although Giusto et al. (2021) did not find a direct association between maternal confidence and ED use, their study reinforced the importance of maternal psychosocial resources and socioeconomic factors in shaping healthcare-seeking behaviors (Giusto et al., 2021). Additionally, Brooks et al. (2015) identified maternal depressive symptoms as predictors of higher healthcare expenditures, including increased ED costs, among publicly insured children with chronic health conditions (Brooks et al., 2015). All of these studies, however, used small or high-risk samples and generally focused on younger pediatric populations.

While the existing literature has explored broader trends in pediatric ED use and maternal MH in high-risk populations, there remain gaps around how, if at all, this might present in a nationally representative dataset with children from a greater range of ages. This study aims to address this gap using 2022-23 National Survey of Children’s Health (NSCH) data to answer the following research question: Among children aged 0-17 years in the US, what is the estimated causal effect of maternal MH status on pediatric ED utilization in the past 12 months?

*Theoretical Background*

This study is grounded in Family Systems Theory and Levesque’s Conceptual Framework of Access to Healthcare. Family Systems Theory describes families as complex, interconnected, and ever-changing systems where changes to an individual member reverberate throughout the group (Hammond, Robert et al., 2015; Lang, 2022). Applied to this context, when a parent experiences mental or physical health (PH) challenges, it may disrupt family roles, shift attention away from children, and leave them undersupported. Levesque et al.’s (2013) Conceptual Framework of Access to Healthcare provides structure in understanding how parents’ perceptions and circumstances shape children’s access to timely and appropriate health care (Levesque et al., 2013).

Together, these frameworks describe how maternal well-being may shape a child’s use of emergency care (see **Figure 1**). Based on Family Systems Theory and Levesque’s Conceptual Framework of Access to Healthcare, we hypothesize that children of mothers with poorer MH (i.e., Fair/Poor) will have children visited the ED more in the past year.

***Figure 1.** Conceptual framework of how maternal health affects child emergency department utilization.*

## Research Question and Hypotheses

*Primary Research Question*

The primary research question is: Among children aged 0-17 years in the US, what is the causal effect of maternal MH status on pediatric ED utilization in the past 12 months? Specifically, we define the treatment as maternal MH status (Fair/Poor vs. Excellent/Very Good/Good), and the outcome as the frequency of caregiver-reported child ED visits in the past year. Notably, this is the number of ED visits for a randomly selected child in the household (please see **Setting and Population** for more details).

*Estimands*

The primary estimand of interest is the average treatment effect (ATE) of poorer maternal MH on pediatric ED utilization.

As a secondary objective, we will estimate the conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) to examine whether the effect of maternal MH varies across key subgroups including child health status, household socioeconomic status, and family structure.

*Hypotheses*

Our primary hypothesis is that children of mothers with Fair/Poor MH will have higher levels of ED utilization compared to children of mothers with Excellent/Very Good/Good MH, under a causal interpretation.

Our secondary hypotheses revolve around the presence of heterogenous treatment effects (HTE) and are as follows:

1.  The effect of maternal MH on ED utilization will be stronger among children in poorer overall health.
2.  The effect will be more pronounced among children in lower-income households.
3.  Family structure (e.g., single-parent households) will modify the relationship between maternal MH and ED utilization.

These hypotheses are informed by prior findings suggesting that maternal MH may both directly influence healthcare-seeking behaviors and interact with broader structural and family-level factors to shape access to care.

## Setting and Population

*National Survey of Children’s Health (NSCH)*

This study will use data from the 2022-2023 NSCH, a nationally representative, cross-sectional survey that explores the physical, emotional, and behavioral health of children aged 0-17 in the US, particularly children with special healthcare needs. The survey also captures key indicators related to access and quality of health care, family and neighborhood characteristics, and other social determinants of health.

Data for the 2022-23 NSCH were collected between July 2022 and January 2023 by the Health Resources and Services Administration’s Maternal and Child Health Bureau. Households were randomly sampled from the Census Master Address File and invited to complete an initial screening questionnaire (available online, on paper, or by phone) to identify the presence of children in the home.(U.S. Census Bureau, 2023) One child per eligible household was randomly selected to be the subject of a detailed age-specific topical questionnaire. Oversampling methods were used to ensure adequate representation of children aged 0-5 and those with special health care needs.(U.S. Census Bureau, 2023)

*Analytic Sample*

The analytic sample will include children with complete data on maternal MH, ED utilization, and all covariates required for the identification strategy. Consistent with prior analyses, survey weights, strata, and clustering will be incorporated to account for the complex survey design and to produce nationally representative estimates.

Although the underlying NSCH data are observational and cross-sectional, this pre-analysis plan conceptualizes a hypothetical causal study in which maternal MH is treated as the exposure of interest. Under standard identification assumptions, we aim to estimate the causal effect of maternal MH on pediatric ED utilization by adjusting for observed covariates.

## Experimental Design

*Assumptions*

To interpret the estimates effects as causal, this study relies on several key identification assumptions:

::: callout-tip
1.  **Exchangeability (i.e., no unmeasured confounding)**
:::

Conditional on the observed covariates included in the adjustment set (e.g., socioeconomic status, family structure), maternal MH is assumed to be independent of potential outcomes in pediatric ED utilization. This assumption may be violated if there are unobserved factors (i.e., those that were not captured in the NSCH dataset) that influence both maternal MH and healthcare utilization.

::: callout-tip
2.  **Positivity**
:::

All individuals have a non-zero probability of being in either maternal MH group (Fair/Poor vs. Excellent/Very Good/Good) across levels of observed covariates. While the NSCH provides a large, nationally representative sample, the relatively small proportion of mothers reporting Fair/Poor mental health (see **Table 1**) may pose challenges for overlap in certain subgroups.

::: callout-tip
3.  **Consistency**
:::

The observed outcome for each child corresponds to the potential outcome under their observed maternal MH status. This assumes that maternal MH is well-defined and consistently measured across respondents.

*Randomization Strategy*

Because this study relies on observational survey data, treatment assignment is not randomized. Instead, this pre-analysis plan conceptualizes a hypothetical target trial in which maternal MH is the exposure of interest. We approximate randomization using Double Machine Learning (DML), a flexible and data-driven approach. This approach aims to reduce bias due to observed confounding by flexibly modeling both the treatment assignment mechanism and the outcome.

*Treatment Arms*

The treatment is defined as maternal MH status, operationalized as a binary exposure:

-   **Treatment group:** Mothers reporting Fair or Poor MH

-   **Control group:** Mothers reporting Excellent, Very Good, or Good MH

This classification is consistent with prior analyses (including one that used NSCH data: Hinojosa et al., 2012, and one that did not: Pfefferle & Spitznagel, 2009) and reflects a meaningful contrast between mothers experiencing poorer MH and those with relatively better MH.

*Timeline*

The NSCH data are cross-sectional, with all variables measured in the same survey period. Additionally, the maternal MH question refers to current mental health status while the ED utilization question refers to ED usage in the past 12 months. As such, the temporal ordering of maternal MH and pediatric ED utilization cannot be definitively established.

In our hypothetical causal framework, we assume that maternal MH precedes pediatric ED utilization within the past 12 months. However, reverse causality, where increased child healthcare needs lead to deteriorated maternal MH, remains a key threat to identification and will be addressed in sensitivity analyses.

## Identification Strategy and Power Analysis

*Identification Strategy*

As previously described, this study is grounded in a causal framework informed by Family Systems Theory and Levesque’s Conceptual Framework of Access to Healthcare. We conceptualize maternal MH as the exposure and pediatric ED utilization as the outcome. A directed acyclic graph (DAG) was developed to identify the minimally sufficient adjustment set required to estimate the causal effect of maternal MH on ED utilization (see **Figure 2)**.

***Figure 2.** Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) demonstrating assumed relationships between variables.*

Based on this DAG, we have identified the following variables as potential confounders:

-   Household socioeconomic status (based on the federal poverty level)

-   Family structure

-   Insurance instability

-   Maternal physical health

-   Paternal mental and physical health

In contrast, variables related to healthcare utilization and access, such as foregone needed care and preventive medical visits, are conceptualized as mediators, as maternal MH may influence these behaviors, which could in turn affect ED utilization. Adjusting for these variables might block part of the causal pathway and bias effect estimates toward the null.

Child health status (labeled as an “other variable” in **Figure 2**) is more complicated. Poor child health may increase maternal psychological distress while also directly increasing ED utilization, meaning it would act as a confounder. However, maternal MH may also influence child health through caregiving behaviors and healthcare engagement, meaning it would act as a mediator. Given this dual role, child health status will not be included in the primary adjustment set but will be incorporated in sensitivity and heterogeneity analyses.

*Power Analysis*

Because this study uses an existing, nationally representative secondary dataset rather than prospectively collecting new data, the purpose of the power analysis is not to determine a required sample size in advance. Rather, we aim to assess whether the available analytic sample is likely to provide sufficient statistical power to detect a meaningful effect on maternal MH on pediatric ED utilization.

Power will be evaluated using a simulation-based minimum detectable effect (MDE) approach. For each candidate effect size, repeated simulations will be used to estimate the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis at a two-sided alpha level of 0.05. The MDE will be defined as the smallest true effect size that yields at least 80% power under the assumed data-generating process. Power for the HTE analyses is expected to be lower than that for the primary ATE analysis, particularly in smaller subgroups. Accordingly, subgroup and CATE findings will be interpreted as secondary and potentially exploratory unless adequate subgroup sample sizes are observed. The primary inferential focus of the study will remain on the overall ATE.

**Figure 3** contains a sample R script for setting up analysis and **Figure 4** contains a sample R script for MDE calculation. All sample scripts in this document were created by looking at HPM 883 course materials and revising them with the support of ChatGPT Instant 5.3.

From a prior analysis, the 2022-23 NSCH yields an analytic sample of 78,380 children/mothers with complete data on the exposure, outcome, and covariates of interest (see **Table 1**). Maternal MH is relatively imbalanced across groups, with approximately 6.5% of mothers reporting Fair/Poor MH. However, a formal power analysis will be conducted in the full empirical analysis following this pre-analysis plan. 

For this assignment, we will synthesize data that mirrors partially cleaned 2022-23 NSCH data from a prior assignment and analysis (**Tables 1 and 2**). Synthesized variables will be created to mimic those from the actual NSCH dataset, including through the response options.

***Figure 3.** Sample R code for setting up analysis.*

```{r, eval=TRUE}
#Use renv package for replicability
renv::restore()

#Load packages

library(tidyverse)
library(data.table)
library(DoubleML)
library(mlr3)
library(mlr3learners)
library(ranger)
library(glmnet)
library(xgboost)
library(tidyverse)
library(data.table)

set.seed(883)

# Sample size: Use actual NSCH sample size - see Table
n <- 78380

# ============================================================================
# 1. OUTCOME VARIABLES
# ============================================================================

# ED visits (ordinal): 0 / 1 / 2-3 / 4+
# Distribution from NSCH: ~70% had 0 visits, ~15% had 1, ~10% had 2-3, ~5% had 4+
ed_visits_ord <- sample(
  x = c(0, 1, 2, 3),
  size = n,
  prob = c(0.70, 0.15, 0.10, 0.05),
  replace = TRUE
)

# Binary ED visit outcome (any visit in past 12 months)
any_ed_visit <- as.numeric(ed_visits_ord > 0)

# ============================================================================
# 2. TREATMENT VARIABLE
# ============================================================================

# Maternal Mental Health: Fair/Poor vs. Excellent/Very Good/Good
# Distribution: ~6.5% report Fair/Poor MH (from proposal: treat_prob = 0.065)
maternal_mh_fp <- rbinom(n = n, size = 1, prob = 0.065)

# ============================================================================
# 3. CONFOUNDERS - MAIN ADJUSTMENT SET
# ============================================================================

# 3a. Federal Poverty Level (FPL) Category
# Categories: <100% FPL, 100-200% FPL, 200-400% FPL, >=400% FPL
# Distribution from NSCH: roughly 20%, 25%, 30%, 25%
fpl_cat <- factor(
  sample(
    x = c("<100%", "100-200%", "200-400%", ">=400%"),
    size = n,
    prob = c(0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.25),
    replace = TRUE
  ),
  levels = c("<100%", "100-200%", "200-400%", ">=400%")
)

# 3b. Family Structure
# Categories: Two-parent household, Single-parent household, Other
# Distribution: ~70% two-parent, ~25% single-parent, ~5% other
family_structure <- factor(
  sample(
    x = c("Two-parent", "Single-parent", "Other"),
    size = n,
    prob = c(0.70, 0.25, 0.05),
    replace = TRUE
  ),
  levels = c("Two-parent", "Single-parent", "Other")
)

# 3c. Insurance Instability
# Binary: Had gap in coverage or unstable insurance
# Distribution: ~15% experienced insurance instability
insurance_instability <- rbinom(n = n, size = 1, prob = 0.15)

# 3d. Maternal Physical Health
# Ordinal scale: Excellent, Very Good, Good, Fair, Poor
# Distribution: ~40% Excellent, ~35% Very Good, ~20% Good, ~4% Fair, ~1% Poor
maternal_physical_health <- factor(
  sample(
    x = c("Excellent", "Very Good", "Good", "Fair", "Poor"),
    size = n,
    prob = c(0.40, 0.35, 0.20, 0.04, 0.01),
    replace = TRUE
  ),
  levels = c("Excellent", "Very Good", "Good", "Fair", "Poor"),
  ordered = TRUE
)

# 3e. Paternal Mental Health
# Ordinal scale: Same as maternal
# Distribution: ~45% Excellent, ~30% Very Good, ~18% Good, ~5% Fair, ~2% Poor
paternal_mental_health <- factor(
  sample(
    x = c("Excellent", "Very Good", "Good", "Fair", "Poor"),
    size = n,
    prob = c(0.45, 0.30, 0.18, 0.05, 0.02),
    replace = TRUE
  ),
  levels = c("Excellent", "Very Good", "Good", "Fair", "Poor"),
  ordered = TRUE
)

# 3f. Paternal Physical Health
# Ordinal scale: Same as maternal
# Distribution: ~42% Excellent, ~32% Very Good, ~19% Good, ~5% Fair, ~2% Poor
paternal_physical_health <- factor(
  sample(
    x = c("Excellent", "Very Good", "Good", "Fair", "Poor"),
    size = n,
    prob = c(0.42, 0.32, 0.19, 0.05, 0.02),
    replace = TRUE
  ),
  levels = c("Excellent", "Very Good", "Good", "Fair", "Poor"),
  ordered = TRUE
)

# ============================================================================
# 4. HTE VARIABLES
# ============================================================================

# 4a. Child Health Status
# Ordinal scale: Excellent, Very Good, Good, Fair, Poor
# Distribution: ~42% Excellent, ~30% Very Good, ~20% Good, ~6% Fair, ~2% Poor
child_health_status <- factor(
  sample(
    x = c("Excellent", "Very Good", "Good", "Fair", "Poor"),
    size = n,
    prob = c(0.42, 0.30, 0.20, 0.06, 0.02),
    replace = TRUE
  ),
  levels = c("Excellent", "Very Good", "Good", "Fair", "Poor"),
  ordered = TRUE
)

# ============================================================================
# 5. MEDIATOR VARIABLES (for sensitivity analysis)
# ============================================================================

# Foregone needed care (binary)
foregone_care <- rbinom(n = n, size = 1, prob = 0.08)

# Preventive medical visits (binary: had well-child visit in past year)
preventive_visits <- rbinom(n = n, size = 1, prob = 0.75)

# ============================================================================
# 6. COMBINE INTO DATAFRAME
# ============================================================================

nsch_df <- tibble(
  # Outcome variables
  ed_visits_ord,
  any_ed_visit,
  # Treatment
  maternal_mh_fp,
  # Main confounders
  fpl_cat,
  family_structure,
  insurance_instability,
  maternal_physical_health,
  paternal_mental_health,
  paternal_physical_health,
  # HTE variables
  child_health_status,
  # Mediators
  foregone_care,
  preventive_visits
)

# Create analysis dataset with complete cases
analysis_df <- nsch_df %>%
  select(all_of(c("ed_visits_ord", "any_ed_visit", "maternal_mh_fp", 
                    "fpl_cat", "family_structure", "insurance_instability",
                    "maternal_physical_health", "paternal_mental_health", 
                    "paternal_physical_health", "child_health_status"))) %>%
  drop_na()

# Convert to data.table for later use
analysis_dt <- as.data.table(analysis_df)

# ============================================================================
# 7. INSPECT SYNTHETIC DATA
# ============================================================================

# Check sample size
nrow(analysis_df)

# Check distributions
summary(analysis_df)

# Cross-tabulations
table(analysis_df$maternal_mh_fp) 
#Setting seed at 883 should yield 73,259  participants with good maternal MH and 5,121 participants with poor maternal MH. Of note, this is slightly off but very close to the values observed in the true NSCH 2022-23 dataset (see Table 1).
table(analysis_df$ed_visits_ord)
table(analysis_df$maternal_mh_fp, analysis_df$any_ed_visit)
table(analysis_df$fpl_cat)
table(analysis_df$family_structure)

# Proportions
prop.table(table(analysis_df$maternal_mh_fp))
prop.table(table(analysis_df$any_ed_visit))
prop.table(table(analysis_df$fpl_cat))
```

***Figure 4.** Sample R code for power and MDE analysis with simulated data.*

```{r, eval=TRUE}
# ============================================================================
# FIGURE 4: FASTER POWER ANALYSIS - For Testing/Exploration
# ============================================================================

# Use FEWER and SIMPLER models for quick iteration
simulate_power_once_fast <- function(data,
                                     true_ate = 0.10,
                                     alpha = 0.05) {
  
  # Get sample size from data
  n <- nrow(data)
  
  # Extract variables - properly convert to data frame
  data_df <- as.data.frame(data)
  
  y_orig <- data_df$any_ed_visit
  d_orig <- data_df$maternal_mh_fp
  
  # Get covariate columns
  x_vars <- c("fpl_cat", "family_structure", "insurance_instability",
              "maternal_physical_health", "paternal_mental_health", 
              "paternal_physical_health")
  
  # Extract covariates
  X <- data_df[, x_vars, drop = FALSE]
  
  # Generate treatment effect
  y_sim <- y_orig
  treated_indices <- which(d_orig == 1)
  if (length(treated_indices) > 0) {
    for (i in treated_indices) {
      new_prob <- min(y_orig[i] + true_ate, 1)
      y_sim[i] <- rbinom(1, 1, new_prob)
    }
  }
  
  # Prepare data frame for DoubleML
  dml_df <- data.frame(
    Y = y_sim,
    D = d_orig,
    X
  )
  
  # Create DoubleMLData object
  dml_data <- DoubleMLData$new(
    data = dml_df,
    y_col = "Y",
    d_cols = "D",
    x_cols = x_vars
  )
  
  # FASTER LEARNERS: Fewer trees, bigger min node size, fewer folds
  ml_g <- lrn("regr.ranger", num.trees = 100, min.node.size = 20)
  ml_m <- lrn("classif.ranger", num.trees = 100, min.node.size = 20, predict_type = "prob")
  
  # Fit IRM with fewer folds
  dml_irm <- DoubleMLIRM$new(
    data = dml_data,
    ml_g = ml_g,
    ml_m = ml_m,
    n_folds = 3,  # Reduced from 5 to 3
    n_rep = 1,
    score = "ATE"
  )
  
  # Fit and extract p-value
  dml_irm$fit()
  pval <- dml_irm$summary()$pval[1]
  
  # Return 1 if null rejected, 0 otherwise
  return(as.numeric(pval < alpha))
}

# ============================================================================
# RUN FAST POWER ANALYSIS
# ============================================================================

effect_grid <- seq(0.02, 0.15, by = 0.02)
n_sims <- 3  # Reduced from 5

cat("Starting FAST power analysis with", length(effect_grid), "effect sizes and", 
    n_sims, "simulations per effect size...\n")
cat("Expected runtime: ~5-10 minutes\n\n")

start_time <- Sys.time()

power_results <- map_dfr(effect_grid, function(eff) {
  cat("Testing effect size =", eff, "...")
  
  rejects <- replicate(
    n_sims,
    tryCatch(
      simulate_power_once_fast(
        data = analysis_df_numeric,
        true_ate = eff
      ),
      error = function(e) {
        cat("\n  Error:", conditionMessage(e), "\n")
        NA
      }
    )
  )
  
  power <- mean(rejects, na.rm = TRUE)
  n_successful <- sum(!is.na(rejects))
  
  cat(" Power =", round(power, 3), "(",  n_successful, "/", n_sims, "successful)\n")
  
  tibble(
    effect_size = eff,
    power = power,
    n_successful_sims = n_successful,
    n_total_sims = n_sims
  )
})

end_time <- Sys.time()
runtime <- difftime(end_time, start_time, units = "mins")

cat("\n=== POWER ANALYSIS RESULTS ===\n")
cat("Total runtime:", round(as.numeric(runtime), 1), "minutes\n\n")
print(power_results)

# ============================================================================
# MDE AND VISUALIZATION (same as before)
# ============================================================================

mde_result <- power_results %>%
  filter(power >= 0.80) %>%
  slice(1)

cat("\n=== MINIMUM DETECTABLE EFFECT (MDE) ===\n\n")
if (nrow(mde_result) > 0) {
  cat("MDE:", round(mde_result$effect_size, 3), "\n")
  cat("Power at MDE:", round(mde_result$power, 3), "\n")
} else {
  cat("No effect size achieved 80% power.\n")
  cat("Max power observed:", round(max(power_results$power), 3), "\n")
}

# Visualization
power_plot <- power_results %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = effect_size, y = power)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", size = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Power Curve: Effect Size vs Statistical Power",
    subtitle = paste("n =", nrow(analysis_df), ", simulations =", n_sims),
    x = "Effect Size",
    y = "Statistical Power"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  ylim(0, 1)

print(power_plot)
```

## Estimation Strategy

This study will estimate the causal effect of maternal MH on pediatric ED usage using DML. DML is a semi-parametric approach that combines ML methods with causal inference techniques to obtain unbiased estimates of treatment effects in the presence of high-dimensional covariates. Given the binary nature of the exposure, we will implement the Interactive Regression Model (IRM) framework, which is well-suited for estimating ATEs in this setting.

*Double Machine Learning Framework*

The DML approach is composed of two primary components:

1.  **Treatment model (propensity score):** The probability of a mother having Fair/Poor MH conditional on observed covariates.
2.  **Outcome model:** The expected level of pediatric ED utilization conditional on maternal MH status and observed covariates.

As previously stated, the primary estimand is the ATE of poorer maternal MH (Fair/Poor) compared to better maternal MH (Excellent/Very Good/Good) on pediatric ED utilization in the past 12 months. Formally, this is defined as the difference in expected outcomes under the two potential treatment states:

*ATE = E\[Y(1) - Y(0)\]*

Where *Y(1)* represents ED utilization if maternal MH is Fair/Poor, and *Y(0)* represents ED utilization if maternal MH is Excellent/Very Good/Good.

*Covariate Adjustment*

The covariates included in the DML procedure are informed by the identification strategy and DAG. The primary adjustment set includes:

-   Household socioeconomic status (based on the federal poverty level)

-   Family structure

-   Insurance instability

-   Maternal physical health

-   Paternal mental and physical health

Variables identified as mediators (i.e., foregone needed care and preventive medical visits) will be excluded from the primary adjustment set to avoid blocking causal pathways. Child health status will be excluded from the main specification due to its ambiguous role as both a potential confounder and mediator but will be included in the secondary and sensitivity analyses.

*Outcome Specification*

The primary outcome, pediatric ED utilization, will be modeled as an ordinal variable capturing the number of ED visits in the past 12 months (0, 1, 2-3, or 4+ visits). For the purposes of DML implementation, we will also estimate models using a binary outcome (any ED visit vs. none) to support interpretation and ensure robustness across outcome specifications.

*Estimation Strategy Overview and Code*

**Figure 5** estimates the propensity score, defined as the probability a mother reports Fair/Poor MH conditional on observed covariates. The model includes all variables in the primary adjustment set identified through the DAG ( e.g., socioeconomic status, family structure). We will assess the positivity assumption by examining overlap between the treatment group using a histogram.

***Figure 5.** Sample R code for propensity score estimation and histogram to check overlap.*

```{r, eval=TRUE}
# ============================================================================
# FIGURE 5: PROPENSITY SCORE ESTIMATION & OVERLAP DIAGNOSTICS
# ============================================================================

# Step 1: Prepare data for propensity score model
# Convert factors to numeric for ranger compatibility

ps_df <- analysis_df %>%
  select(all_of(c(treat_var, x_vars_main))) %>%
  mutate(
    # Convert all factors to numeric (ordinal encoding)
    across(where(is.factor), as.numeric),
    # Ensure treatment is numeric 0/1
    !!treat_var := as.numeric(!!sym(treat_var))
  )

# Step 2: Fit propensity score model using Random Forest
# This estimates P(Treatment = 1 | X)

cat("Fitting propensity score model using Random Forest (Ranger)...\n")

ps_formula <- as.formula(
  paste(treat_var, "~", paste(x_vars_main, collapse = " + "))
)

ps_model <- ranger(
  formula = ps_formula,
  data = ps_df,
  probability = TRUE,      # For classification probabilities
  num.trees = 500,
  min.node.size = 10,
  seed = 883,
  verbose = FALSE
)

# Step 3: Extract propensity score predictions
# For binary treatment, get P(Treatment = 1)

ps_pred <- predict(ps_model, data = ps_df)$predictions

# Handle different output formats from ranger
if (is.matrix(ps_pred)) {
  # If matrix, extract column for treatment = 1
  ps_pred <- ps_pred[, "1"]
} else if (is.vector(ps_pred)) {
  # Already a vector of probabilities
  ps_pred <- ps_pred
}

# Step 4: Add propensity scores to dataframe and compute overlap diagnostics

ps_df_aug <- ps_df %>%
  mutate(
    propensity_score = ps_pred,
    treatment = !!sym(treat_var)
  )

# Step 5: Examine propensity score distribution

cat("\n=== PROPENSITY SCORE SUMMARY ===\n")
print(summary(ps_df_aug$propensity_score))

cat("\nBy Treatment Group:\n")
print(
  ps_df_aug %>%
    group_by(treatment) %>%
    summarize(
      n = n(),
      mean_ps = mean(propensity_score),
      sd_ps = sd(propensity_score),
      min_ps = min(propensity_score),
      max_ps = max(propensity_score),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
)

# Step 6: Visualize propensity score overlap

ps_plot <- ps_df_aug %>%
  mutate(Treatment = factor(treatment, labels = c("Excellent/VG/Good MH", "Fair/Poor MH"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = propensity_score, fill = Treatment)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5, adjust = 1.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue", "lavender")) +
  labs(
    title = "Propensity Score Distribution by Maternal Mental Health Status",
    subtitle = "Assessment of positivity assumption (common support)",
    x = "Estimated Propensity Score P(Fair/Poor MH | X)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Maternal MH"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray40"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

print(ps_plot)

# Step 7: Flag regions of poor overlap (for sensitivity analysis)

ps_df_aug <- ps_df_aug %>%
  mutate(
    poor_overlap = case_when(
      propensity_score < 0.01 ~ "Very Poor (< 0.01)",
      propensity_score > 0.99 ~ "Very Poor (> 0.99)",
      propensity_score < 0.05 ~ "Weak (0.01-0.05)",
      propensity_score > 0.95 ~ "Weak (0.95-0.99)",
      TRUE ~ "Good"
    )
  )

cat("\n=== OVERLAP REGION ASSESSMENT ===\n")
overlap_table <- table(ps_df_aug$poor_overlap)
print(overlap_table)

cat("\nPercentage in regions of concern:\n")
print(
  prop.table(overlap_table) * 100 %>% round(2)
)

# Step 8: Create summary visualizations for positivity assessment

overlap_summary <- ps_df_aug %>%
  group_by(treatment, poor_overlap) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(treatment = factor(treatment, labels = c("Excellent/VG/Good MH", "Fair/Poor MH")))

overlap_plot <- overlap_summary %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = poor_overlap, y = n, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue", "lavender")) +
  labs(
    title = "Sample Distribution Across Propensity Score Regions",
    x = "Overlap Quality",
    y = "Count",
    fill = "Maternal MH",
    subtitle = "Assessing positivity: overlap between treatment groups across covariate space"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray40"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

print(overlap_plot)

# Step 9: Save propensity scores for sensitivity analysis
# These will be used later in trimming to common support region

cat("\nPropensity score model fitted successfully.\n")
cat("Propensity scores saved for use in downstream analyses.\n")

# Store for later use
ps_scores_for_trim <- ps_df_aug %>%
  select(propensity_score, treatment) %>%
  bind_cols(original_index = 1:nrow(ps_df_aug))

```

**Figures 6 and 7** contain the R scripts for the primary estimation strategy. First, we will use an IRM, which is better suited for binary treatment variables, to look at the relationship between maternal MH and child ED visits (yes/no). next (, we will use a partially linear regression model (PLR), which is more often used for continuous outcomes, to assess the relationship between maternal MH and the ordinal child ED utilization variable.

The two nuisance models estimated are 1. The outcome model estimating expected ED utilization conditional on covariates and treatment, and 2. A treatment model estimating the propensity score. Both models use random forests (via the ‘ranger’ package in R). To reduce overfitting, the DML estimator uses cross-fitting, in which data are divided into folds and nuisance models will be trained on one subset of data and evaluated on another.

***Figure 6.** Sample R code for estimation strategy – Part 1: Main ATE with binary maternal MH outcome.*

```{r, eval=TRUE}
# ============================================================================
# FIGURE 6: DOUBLE MACHINE LEARNING - PART 1
# Main ATE Estimation with Binary Outcome (any ED visit)
# ============================================================================

cat("\n========== DOUBLE MACHINE LEARNING: BINARY OUTCOME ==========\n")

# Step 1: Prepare data for DoubleML with binary outcome
# Convert all variables to numeric format for DML compatibility

dml_df_bin <- analysis_df %>%
  select(all_of(c(outcome_binary_var, treat_var, x_vars_main))) %>%
  # Convert factors to numeric
  mutate(
    across(where(is.factor), as.numeric)
  ) %>%
  # Rename for DML (Y = outcome, D = treatment)
  rename(
    Y = all_of(outcome_binary_var),
    D = all_of(treat_var)
  ) %>%
  # Verify no missing data
  drop_na()

cat("Sample size for DML analysis (binary outcome):", nrow(dml_df_bin), "\n")
cat("Treatment prevalence:", round(mean(dml_df_bin$D), 4), "\n")
cat("Outcome prevalence (any ED visit):", round(mean(dml_df_bin$Y), 4), "\n\n")

# Step 2: Create DoubleMLData object
# This structures the data for DML estimation

dml_data_bin <- DoubleMLData$new(
  data = dml_df_bin,
  y_col = "Y",                    # Outcome column
  d_cols = "D",                   # Treatment column
  x_cols = x_vars_main            # Covariate columns (from adjustment set)
)

cat("DoubleMLData object created successfully.\n")
cat("Outcome variable: Y (", outcome_binary_var, ")\n", sep = "")
cat("Treatment variable: D (", treat_var, ")\n", sep = "")
cat("Adjustment set covariates (", length(x_vars_main), "):\n", sep = "")
cat("  -", paste(x_vars_main, collapse = "\n  - "), "\n\n")

# Step 3: Specify machine learning learners for nuisance parameters
# ml_g: outcome model E[Y | X, D]
# ml_m: treatment model (propensity score) P(D = 1 | X)

cat("Specifying machine learning learners...\n")

# Outcome model: Random Forest for regression
ml_g_bin <- lrn("regr.ranger", 
                num.trees = 500,        # Number of trees
                min.node.size = 5,      # Minimum node size
                max.depth = 15,         # Maximum depth
                mtry = ceiling(sqrt(length(x_vars_main))))  # Number of variables to sample

# Treatment model: Random Forest for classification
ml_m_bin <- lrn("classif.ranger",
                num.trees = 500,
                min.node.size = 5,
                max.depth = 15,
                predict_type = "prob",  # Return probabilities
                mtry = ceiling(sqrt(length(x_vars_main))))

cat("ML learners configured:\n")
cat("  - Outcome model: Random Forest (Ranger) with", 500, "trees\n")
cat("  - Treatment model: Random Forest (Ranger) with", 500, "trees\n\n")

# Step 4: Initialize DoubleML IRM (Interactive Regression Model)
# IRM is appropriate for binary treatments with ATE score

cat("Initializing DoubleML IRM model...\n")

dml_irm_bin <- DoubleMLIRM$new(
  data = dml_data_bin,
  ml_g = ml_g_bin,               # Outcome model learner
  ml_m = ml_m_bin,               # Treatment model learner
  n_folds = 5,                   # 5-fold cross-fitting
  n_rep = 1,                     # Single repetition
  score = "ATE",                 # Average Treatment Effect score
  dml_procedure = "dml2"         # Neyman orthogonality procedure
)

cat("DML IRM model initialized successfully.\n\n")

# Step 5: Fit the model
# This performs cross-fitting and estimates the nuisance parameters

cat("Fitting DML model (this may take a minute)...\n")

dml_irm_bin$fit(store_predictions = TRUE)

cat("Model fitted successfully!\n\n")

# Step 6: Extract and display results

cat("========== MAIN RESULTS: BINARY OUTCOME ==========\n\n")

# Get summary table
summary_bin <- dml_irm_bin$summary()
print(summary_bin)

# Extract key quantities
ate_est_bin <- dml_irm_bin$coef[1]
ate_se_bin <- dml_irm_bin$se[1]
ate_ci_bin <- dml_irm_bin$confint()

cat("\n========== INTERPRETED RESULTS ==========\n")
cat("Average Treatment Effect (ATE):", round(ate_est_bin, 4), "\n")
cat("Standard Error:", round(ate_se_bin, 4), "\n")
cat("95% Confidence Interval: [", 
    round(ate_ci_bin[1, 1], 4), ", ", 
    round(ate_ci_bin[1, 2], 4), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("P-value:", round(summary_bin$pval[1], 4), "\n\n")

# Interpretation
cat("INTERPRETATION:\n")
cat("Children of mothers with Fair/Poor mental health are estimated to have\n")
cat(sprintf("a %.2f%% (%.2f percentage point) ", ate_est_bin * 100, ate_est_bin),
    "higher probability of any ED visit\n")
cat("in the past 12 months compared to children of mothers with\n")
cat("Excellent/Very Good/Good mental health, after adjusting for covariates.\n\n")

if (summary_bin$pval[1] < 0.05) {
  cat("This effect is STATISTICALLY SIGNIFICANT at the 0.05 level.\n")
} else {
  cat("This effect is NOT statistically significant at the 0.05 level.\n")
}

cat("\n")

# Step 7: Create results table

results_tbl_bin <- tibble(
  Estimand = "Average Treatment Effect (ATE)",
  Estimate = ate_est_bin,
  Std_Error = ate_se_bin,
  CI_Lower = ate_ci_bin[1, 1],
  CI_Upper = ate_ci_bin[1, 2],
  P_Value = summary_bin$pval[1],
  Significant = ifelse(summary_bin$pval[1] < 0.05, "Yes***", "No")
)

cat("========== RESULTS TABLE ==========\n")
print(results_tbl_bin)

# Step 8: Diagnostic plots

cat("\n========== DIAGNOSTIC PLOTS ==========\n")

# Plot 1: Predicted values vs residuals
predictions_bin <- dml_irm_bin$predictions

pred_resid_plot <- tibble(
  predicted = predictions_bin$ml_g0,
  residuals = predictions_bin$ml_g0 - dml_df_bin$Y
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = predicted, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Residual Plot: Outcome Model Diagnostics",
    x = "Predicted ED Visit Probability",
    y = "Residuals",
    subtitle = "Should show random scatter around y=0 with no patterns"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray40")
  )

print(pred_resid_plot)

# Plot 2: Treatment propensity score overlap
propensity_plot <- tibble(
  propensity = predictions_bin$ml_m,
  treatment = dml_df_bin$D
) %>%
  mutate(treatment = factor(treatment, labels = c("Good MH", "Fair/Poor MH"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = propensity, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, bins = 30, position = "identity") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue", "firebrick")) +
  labs(
    title = "Propensity Score Overlap Assessment",
    x = "Estimated Propensity Score P(Fair/Poor MH | X)",
    y = "Count",
    fill = "Maternal MH",
    subtitle = "Histograms should have substantial overlap"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray40")
  )

print(propensity_plot)

# Step 9: Model comparison with confidence intervals

results_summary <- tibble(
  Model = "Binary Outcome (Main)",
  Method = "DML IRM",
  ATE = ate_est_bin,
  SE = ate_se_bin,
  CI_Lower = ate_ci_bin[1, 1],
  CI_Upper = ate_ci_bin[1, 2],
  P_Value = summary_bin$pval[1]
)

ate_plot <- results_summary %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Model, y = ATE)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = CI_Lower, ymax = CI_Upper), 
                width = 0.2, color = "steelblue", size = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Treatment Effect with 95% Confidence Interval",
    y = "ATE (Probability Increase in ED Visit)",
    x = "",
    subtitle = "Effect of Fair/Poor vs. Excellent/Very Good/Good Maternal MH"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray40"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11)
  ) +
  coord_flip()

print(ate_plot)

# Step 10: Save key results for later use

cat("\n========== MODEL SAVED FOR SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS ==========\n")
cat("dml_irm_bin object contains:\n")
cat("  - Fitted coefficients and standard errors\n")
cat("  - Confidence intervals\n")
cat("  - Predictions for diagnostics\n")
cat("  - Ready for use in sensitivity analyses\n\n")
```

***Figure 7.** Sample R code for estimation strategy – Part 2: Main ATE for ordinal/approximately continuous outcome.*

```{r, eval=TRUE}
# ============================================================================
# FIGURE 7: DOUBLE MACHINE LEARNING - PART 2
# Main ATE Estimation with Ordinal Outcome (ED visit counts: 0/1/2-3/4+)
# ============================================================================

cat("\n========== DOUBLE MACHINE LEARNING: ORDINAL OUTCOME ==========\n")

# Step 1: Prepare data for DoubleML with ordinal outcome
# Outcome coded as: 0, 1, 2, 3 representing 0 / 1 / 2-3 / 4+ visits

dml_df_ord <- analysis_df %>%
  select(all_of(c(outcome_var, treat_var, x_vars_main))) %>%
  # Convert factors to numeric
  mutate(
    across(where(is.factor), as.numeric)
  ) %>%
  # Rename for DML (Y = outcome, D = treatment)
  rename(
    Y = all_of(outcome_var),
    D = all_of(treat_var)
  ) %>%
  # Verify no missing data
  drop_na()

cat("Sample size for DML analysis (ordinal outcome):", nrow(dml_df_ord), "\n")
cat("Treatment prevalence:", round(mean(dml_df_ord$D), 4), "\n")
cat("Outcome distribution (ED visits):\n")

outcome_dist <- table(dml_df_ord$Y)
cat("  0 visits:", outcome_dist["0"], "(", 
    round(100 * outcome_dist["0"] / nrow(dml_df_ord), 1), "%)\n", sep = "")
cat("  1 visit: ", outcome_dist["1"], "(", 
    round(100 * outcome_dist["1"] / nrow(dml_df_ord), 1), "%)\n", sep = "")
cat("  2-3 visits:", outcome_dist["2"], "(", 
    round(100 * outcome_dist["2"] / nrow(dml_df_ord), 1), "%)\n", sep = "")
cat("  4+ visits:", outcome_dist["3"], "(", 
    round(100 * outcome_dist["3"] / nrow(dml_df_ord), 1), "%)\n\n", sep = "")

# Step 2: Create DoubleMLData object for ordinal outcome

dml_data_ord <- DoubleMLData$new(
  data = dml_df_ord,
  y_col = "Y",                    # Outcome column (ordinal: 0,1,2,3)
  d_cols = "D",                   # Treatment column
  x_cols = x_vars_main            # Covariate columns
)

cat("DoubleMLData object created successfully.\n")
cat("Outcome variable: Y (", outcome_var, ") - ordinal scale 0-3\n", sep = "")
cat("Treatment variable: D (", treat_var, ")\n", sep = "")
cat("Adjustment set covariates (", length(x_vars_main), "):\n", sep = "")
cat("  -", paste(x_vars_main, collapse = "\n  - "), "\n\n")

# Step 3: Specify machine learning learners for ordinal outcome
# For ordinal outcomes, we use PLR (Partialling Out / Frisch-Waugh-Lovell)
# ml_l: outcome model E[Y | X, D] - treated as approximately continuous
# ml_m: treatment model (propensity score) P(D = 1 | X)

cat("Specifying machine learning learners for ordinal outcome...\n")

# Outcome model: Random Forest for regression (treats ordinal as continuous)
ml_l_ord <- lrn("regr.ranger",
                num.trees = 500,
                min.node.size = 5,
                max.depth = 15,
                mtry = ceiling(sqrt(length(x_vars_main))))

# Treatment model: Random Forest for classification
ml_m_ord <- lrn("classif.ranger",
                num.trees = 500,
                min.node.size = 5,
                max.depth = 15,
                predict_type = "prob",
                mtry = ceiling(sqrt(length(x_vars_main))))

cat("ML learners configured:\n")
cat("  - Outcome model: Random Forest (Ranger) with", 500, "trees\n")
cat("    (Treats ordinal outcome as approximately continuous)\n")
cat("  - Treatment model: Random Forest (Ranger) with", 500, "trees\n\n")

# Step 4: Initialize DoubleML PLR (Partialling Out / Frisch-Waugh-Lovell)
# PLR is more suitable for continuous/ordinal outcomes
# Uses 'partialling out' score which is robust to nuisance parameter estimation

cat("Initializing DoubleML PLR model...\n")
cat("Note: PLR uses the 'partialling out' orthogonality condition,\n")
cat("which is more robust for continuous/ordinal outcomes.\n\n")

dml_plr_ord <- DoubleMLPLR$new(
  data = dml_data_ord,
  ml_l = ml_l_ord,                # Outcome model learner
  ml_m = ml_m_ord,                # Treatment model learner
  n_folds = 5,                    # 5-fold cross-fitting
  n_rep = 1,                      # Single repetition
  score = "partialling out",      # Partialling out score (recommended for PLR)
  dml_procedure = "dml2"          # Neyman orthogonality procedure
)

cat("DML PLR model initialized successfully.\n\n")

# Step 5: Fit the model

cat("Fitting DML PLR model (this may take a minute)...\n")

dml_plr_ord$fit(store_predictions = TRUE)

cat("Model fitted successfully!\n\n")

# Step 6: Extract and display results

cat("========== MAIN RESULTS: ORDINAL OUTCOME ==========\n\n")

# Get summary table
summary_ord <- dml_plr_ord$summary()
print(summary_ord)

# Extract key quantities
ate_est_ord <- dml_plr_ord$coef[1]
ate_se_ord <- dml_plr_ord$se[1]
ate_ci_ord <- dml_plr_ord$confint()

cat("\n========== INTERPRETED RESULTS ==========\n")
cat("Average Treatment Effect (ATE):", round(ate_est_ord, 4), "\n")
cat("Standard Error:", round(ate_se_ord, 4), "\n")
cat("95% Confidence Interval: [", 
    round(ate_ci_ord[1, 1], 4), ", ", 
    round(ate_ci_ord[1, 2], 4), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("P-value:", round(summary_ord$pval[1], 4), "\n\n")

# Interpretation
cat("INTERPRETATION (Ordinal Scale):\n")
cat("Children of mothers with Fair/Poor mental health are estimated to have\n")
cat(sprintf("a %.4f unit higher ED visit count ", ate_est_ord),
    "(on the 0-3 ordinal scale)\n")
cat("compared to children of mothers with Excellent/Very Good/Good mental health.\n")
cat("This translates to approximately:\n")

# Convert ordinal scale interpretation
ate_ord_pct <- ate_est_ord / 3 * 100  # Scale to percentage of ordinal range
cat(sprintf("  - %.1f%% of the ordinal scale range\n", ate_ord_pct))

if (summary_ord$pval[1] < 0.05) {
  cat("This effect is STATISTICALLY SIGNIFICANT at the 0.05 level.\n")
} else {
  cat("This effect is NOT statistically significant at the 0.05 level.\n")
}

cat("\n")

# Step 7: Create results table

results_tbl_ord <- tibble(
  Estimand = "Average Treatment Effect (ATE)",
  Estimate = ate_est_ord,
  Std_Error = ate_se_ord,
  CI_Lower = ate_ci_ord[1, 1],
  CI_Upper = ate_ci_ord[1, 2],
  P_Value = summary_ord$pval[1],
  Significant = ifelse(summary_ord$pval[1] < 0.05, "Yes***", "No")
)

cat("========== RESULTS TABLE ==========\n")
print(results_tbl_ord)

# Step 8: Diagnostic plots

cat("\n========== DIAGNOSTIC PLOTS ==========\n")

# Plot 1: Predicted values vs residuals for outcome model
predictions_ord <- dml_plr_ord$predictions

pred_resid_plot_ord <- tibble(
  predicted = predictions_ord$ml_l,
  residuals = predictions_ord$ml_l - dml_df_ord$Y
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = predicted, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "blue", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Residual Plot: Outcome Model Diagnostics (Ordinal)",
    x = "Predicted ED Visit Count",
    y = "Residuals",
    subtitle = "Should show random scatter around y=0; loess line should be flat"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray40")
  )

print(pred_resid_plot_ord)

# Plot 2: Distribution of residuals
residual_dist_plot <- tibble(
  residuals = predictions_ord$ml_l - dml_df_ord$Y
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = residuals)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, alpha = 0.7, fill = "steelblue", color = "black") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", size = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Outcome Model Residuals",
    x = "Residuals",
    y = "Frequency",
    subtitle = "Should be approximately symmetric around zero"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray40")
  )

print(residual_dist_plot)

# Plot 3: Treatment propensity score overlap
propensity_plot_ord <- tibble(
  propensity = predictions_ord$ml_m,
  treatment = dml_df_ord$D
) %>%
  mutate(treatment = factor(treatment, labels = c("Good MH", "Fair/Poor MH"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = propensity, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, bins = 30, position = "identity") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue", "firebrick")) +
  labs(
    title = "Propensity Score Overlap (Ordinal Analysis)",
    x = "Estimated Propensity Score P(Fair/Poor MH | X)",
    y = "Count",
    fill = "Maternal MH",
    subtitle = "Histograms should have substantial overlap"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray40")
  )

print(propensity_plot_ord)

# Step 9: Comparison between ordinal and binary results

cat("\n========== COMPARISON WITH BINARY OUTCOME ==========\n")

# Create comparison table
results_comparison <- tibble(
  Outcome = c("Binary (Any ED Visit)", "Ordinal (ED Visit Count)"),
  ATE = c(ate_est_bin, ate_est_ord),
  SE = c(ate_se_bin, ate_se_ord),
  CI_Lower = c(ate_ci_bin[1, 1], ate_ci_ord[1, 1]),
  CI_Upper = c(ate_ci_bin[1, 2], ate_ci_ord[1, 2]),
  P_Value = c(summary_bin$pval[1], summary_ord$pval[1]),
  Significant = c(
    ifelse(summary_bin$pval[1] < 0.05, "Yes***", "No"),
    ifelse(summary_ord$pval[1] < 0.05, "Yes***", "No")
  )
)

print(results_comparison)

cat("\nNote: Binary and ordinal outcomes are estimated using different DML methods\n")
cat("(IRM vs. PLR) and on different scales, so direct comparison requires caution.\n")
cat("Both should point to similar conclusions if the treatment effect is robust.\n\n")

# Step 10: Create comparison forest plot

comparison_plot <- results_comparison %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Outcome, y = ATE)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = CI_Lower, ymax = CI_Upper),
                width = 0.2, color = "steelblue", size = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Treatment Effects: Binary vs. Ordinal Outcomes",
    y = "Average Treatment Effect",
```

## HTE Analysis Plan

To examine whether the effect of maternal MH on pediatric ED utilization varies across subpopulations, we will conduct analyses of HTEs within the DML framework. Specifically, we will estimate subgroup-specific ATEs by fitting the primary DML IRM separately within levels of selected subgroup variables.  

We will evaluate heterogeneity across three a priori subgroup dimensions motivated by theory and prior literature: child health status (poor, fair, good, very good, excellent), household socioeconomic status as measured by FPL category (0-99% FPL, 100-199% FPL, 200-399% FPL, ≥400% FPL), and family structure (single- versus multi-parent structure). For child health status specifically, we will estimate subgroup-specific effects with both dichotomized (poor/fair versus good/very good/excellent) and ordinal versions of child health status. For each subgroup level, we will subset the analytic sample, retain the primary outcome, treatment, and main covariate set, and estimate the ATE of maternal MH on pediatric ED utilization using the same DML specification as the primary analysis.  

Within each subgroup-specific model, we will use the IRM formulation of DML with 5-fold cross-fitting and random forest learners for both the outcome model and treatment model. For each subgroup level, we will report the estimated effect, standard error, 95% confidence interval, and subgroup sample size. Heterogeneity will be assessed descriptively by comparing the magnitude, direction, and precision of effect estimates across subgroup levels.  

These analyses are intended to assess whether the estimated effect of maternal MH is stronger among more vulnerable populations, including children in poorer health, children in lower-income households, and children in single-parent family structures. Because child health status may plausibly function as both an effect modifier and a mediator, heterogeneity analyses involving child health will be interpreted cautiously as exploratory.  

***Figure 9.** Sample R code for HTE analysis.*

```{r, eval=TRUE}
# ============================================================================
# FIGURE 9: HETEROGENEOUS TREATMENT EFFECTS (HTE) ANALYSIS
# Examine whether treatment effects vary across key subgroups
# ============================================================================

cat("\n========== HETEROGENEOUS TREATMENT EFFECTS (HTE) ANALYSIS ==========\n\n")

# Step 1: Define function to estimate subgroup-specific ATEs

cat("Defining function to estimate subgroup-specific treatment effects...\n\n")

estimate_subgroup_ate <- function(data, 
                                  subgroup_var, 
                                  subgroup_level,
                                  outcome_name, 
                                  treat_name, 
                                  x_names,
                                  method = "binary") {
  
  # Filter to subgroup
  sub_df <- data %>%
    filter(.data[[subgroup_var]] == subgroup_level) %>%
    select(all_of(c(outcome_name, treat_name, x_names))) %>%
    drop_na() %>%
    mutate(
      # Convert factors to numeric
      across(where(is.factor), as.numeric)
    ) %>%
    rename(
      Y = all_of(outcome_name),
      D = all_of(treat_name)
    )
  
  # Skip if subgroup too small
  n_sub <- nrow(sub_df)
  if (n_sub < 50) {
    warning(paste("Subgroup", subgroup_level, "has only", n_sub, "observations"))
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # Create DML data object
  dml_data <- DoubleMLData$new(
    data = sub_df,
    y_col = "Y",
    d_cols = "D",
    x_cols = x_names
  )
  
  # Specify learners
  ml_g <- lrn("regr.ranger", num.trees = 300, min.node.size = 10)
  ml_m <- lrn("classif.ranger", num.trees = 300, min.node.size = 10, 
              predict_type = "prob")
  
  # Fit appropriate model
  if (method == "binary") {
    fit <- DoubleMLIRM$new(
      data = dml_data,
      ml_g = ml_g,
      ml_m = ml_m,
      n_folds = 5,
      score = "ATE"
    )
  } else {
    fit <- DoubleMLPLR$new(
      data = dml_data,
      ml_l = ml_g,
      ml_m = ml_m,
      n_folds = 5,
      score = "partialling out"
    )
  }
  
  # Fit model
  tryCatch(
    {
      fit$fit()
      
      # Extract results
      results <- tibble(
        subgroup = subgroup_var,
        level = as.character(subgroup_level),
        estimate = fit$coef[1],
        std_error = fit$se[1],
        ci_lower = fit$confint()[1, 1],
        ci_upper = fit$confint()[1, 2],
        p_value = fit$summary()$pval[1],
        n = n_sub,
        significant = ifelse(fit$summary()$pval[1] < 0.05, "Yes", "No")
      )
      
      return(results)
    },
    error = function(e) {
      warning(paste("Error fitting model for", subgroup_var, "=", subgroup_level, ":", e$message))
      return(NULL)
    }
  )
}

cat("Function defined successfully.\n\n")

# Step 2: HTE by Child Health Status

# Check for income gradient (is effect stronger at lower income levels?)

if (effect_gradient < 0) {
  cat("Interpretation: Effects are STRONGER at LOWER income levels (as hypothesized)\n")
} else {
  cat("Interpretation: Effects are WEAKER at LOWER income levels (contrary to hypothesis)\n")
}
cat("\n")

# Step 4: HTE by Family Structure

cat("=" %>% strrep(70), "\n")
cat("HTE ANALYSIS 3: BY FAMILY STRUCTURE\n")
cat("=" %>% strrep(70), "\n\n")

cat("Hypothesis: Family structure modifies the relationship between maternal MH and ED use.\n\n")

# Get unique levels of family structure
family_levels <- unique(analysis_df$family_structure)

cat("Estimating subgroup effects for family structure types:\n")
cat("  Levels:", paste(family_levels, collapse = ", "), "\n\n")

# Estimate effects for each level
hte_family <- map_dfr(
  family_levels,
  ~estimate_subgroup_ate(
    data = analysis_df,
    subgroup_var = "family_structure",
    subgroup_level = .x,
    outcome_name = outcome_binary_var,
    treat_name = treat_var,
    x_names = x_vars_main,
    method = "binary"
  )
)

# Remove any NULL results
hte_family <- hte_family %>%
  filter(!is.na(estimate))

cat("Results by Family Structure:\n")
print(hte_family)

# Create visualization for family structure HTE
hte_family_plot <- hte_family %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = level, y = estimate, color = significant)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper), 
                width = 0.2, size = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Yes" = "darkgreen", "No" = "gray50")) +
  labs(
    title = "HTE by Family Structure",
    subtitle = "Does treatment effect differ by family composition?",
    x = "Family Structure",
    y = "Average Treatment Effect",
    color = "Significant\n(p < 0.05)",
    caption = paste("n ranges from", min(hte_family$n), "to", max(hte_family$n))
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray40"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "gray90")
  )

print(hte_family_plot)

cat("\nInterpretation: ", nrow(hte_family), " subgroups analyzed.\n")
cat("Significant effects found in ", 
    sum(hte_family$significant == "Yes"), " subgroups.\n\n", sep = "")

# Step 5: Combine all HTE results into master table

cat("=" %>% strrep(70), "\n")
cat("COMPREHENSIVE HTE SUMMARY TABLE\n")
cat("=" %>% strrep(70), "\n\n")

hte_master <- bind_rows(
  hte_child_health %>% mutate(Variable = "Child Health Status"),
  hte_fpl %>% mutate(Variable = "Federal Poverty Level"),
  hte_family %>% mutate(Variable = "Family Structure")
) %>%
  select(Variable, Level = level, N = n, Estimate = estimate,

         P_Value = p_value, Significant = significant) %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(Estimate, SE, CI_Lower, CI_Upper, P_Value), 
           ~round(., 6))
  )

print(hte_master)

# Step 6: Create combined forest plot across all subgroups

cat("\n\nCOMBINED FOREST PLOT: ALL SUBGROUPS\n")
cat("=" %>% strrep(70), "\n\n")

hte_combined_plot <- bind_rows(
  hte_child_health %>%

    x = "Subgroup",
```

## Sensitivity Analysis Plan

To assess the robustness of our findings, we will conduct several sensitivity analyses that examine whether estimated effects are consistent across alternative modeling choices and assumptions.  

First, we will compare results across alternative exposure specifications. In the primary analysis, maternal MH is modeled as a binary outcome. As a sensitivity check, we will re-estimate the effect using an ordinal-coded version of the outcome (i.e., keeping the original variable structure of poor, fair, good, very good, excellent). Comparing estimates across these specifications will help assess whether results are sensitive to how maternal MH is operationalized.  

Second, we will re-fit the primary DML model using an expanded covariate set that includes child health status. As noted in the identification strategy, child health may plausibly function as either a confounder or a mediator in the relationship between maternal MH and pediatric ED utilization. Because of this dual role, child health is excluded from the primary adjustment set. However, including it in a sensitivity analysis will allow us to examine whether the estimated effect is substantively altered when adjusting for this potentially important variable.  

Third, we will assess the robustness of results to the overlap assumption by restricting the analytic sample to observations in the common-support region. Specifically, we will trim observations with estimated propensity scores below 0.01 or above 0.99 and re-estimate the model in the trimmed sample. This analysis will help determine whether the primary findings are driven by observations with very limited comparability across levels of maternal MH status.  

Finally, we will summarize and compare estimates, standard errors, and confidence intervals across the primary and sensitivity specifications. Consistency in the direction and magnitude of estimates across these models will strengthen confidence in the robustness of the findings, whereas meaningful differences will be interpreted as evidence that results may be sensitive to outcome specification, covariate adjustment, or limited overlap.

***Figure 10.** Sample R code for sensitivity analysis.*

```{r, eval=TRUE}
# ============================================================================
# FIGURE 10: SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS PLAN
# Robustness checks across alternative specifications and sample restrictions
# ============================================================================

cat("\n========== SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS ==========\n\n")

# Step 1: Compare main outcome specifications (already fit)

cat("=" %>% strrep(70), "\n")
cat("SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS 1: OUTCOME SPECIFICATION COMPARISON\n")
cat("=" %>% strrep(70), "\n\n")

cat("Testing robustness across two outcome operationalizations:\n")
cat("  1. Binary: Any ED visit (0/1)\n")
cat("  2. Ordinal: ED visit count (0, 1, 2-3, 4+)\n\n")

# Extract results from already-fit models
main_bin_summary <- dml_irm_bin$summary()
main_ord_summary <- dml_plr_ord$summary()

specification_comparison <- tibble(
  Specification = c("Binary Outcome (IRM)", "Ordinal Outcome (PLR)"),
  Method = c("Interactive Regression Model", "Partialling Out"),
  Estimate = c(dml_irm_bin$coef[1], dml_plr_ord$coef[1]),
  SE = c(dml_irm_bin$se[1], dml_plr_ord$se[1]),
  CI_Lower = c(dml_irm_bin$confint()[1, 1], dml_plr_ord$confint()[1, 1]),
  CI_Upper = c(dml_irm_bin$confint()[1, 2], dml_plr_ord$confint()[1, 2]),
  P_Value = c(main_bin_summary$pval[1], main_ord_summary$pval[1]),
  N = c(nrow(dml_df_bin), nrow(dml_df_ord))
)

cat("Results:\n")
print(specification_comparison)

cat("\nInterpretation:\n")
cat("  Main Binary Result (ATE = ", round(specification_comparison$Estimate[1], 4), "): ",
    ifelse(specification_comparison$P_Value[1] < 0.05, "SIGNIFICANT", "NOT SIGNIFICANT"), "\n", sep = "")
cat("  Main Ordinal Result (ATE = ", round(specification_comparison$Estimate[2], 4), "): ",
    ifelse(specification_comparison$P_Value[2] < 0.05, "SIGNIFICANT", "NOT SIGNIFICANT"), "\n\n", sep = "")

if (abs(specification_comparison$Estimate[1] - specification_comparison$Estimate[2]/3) < 0.01) {
  cat("  ✓ Results are CONSISTENT across outcome operationalizations\n")
} else {
  cat("  ⚠ Results differ across outcome operationalizations - investigate further\n")
}

cat("\n")

# Visualization: Outcome specification comparison
outcome_comp_plot <- specification_comparison %>%
  mutate(Specification = factor(Specification, levels = Specification)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Specification, y = Estimate)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = CI_Lower, ymax = CI_Upper),
                width = 0.2, size = 1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(
    title = "Sensitivity Analysis 1: Outcome Specification",
    subtitle = "Robustness across binary vs. ordinal outcome coding",
    y = "Average Treatment Effect (ATE)",
    x = "Outcome Specification",
    caption = "Error bars represent 95% confidence intervals"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray40"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "gray90")
  )

print(outcome_comp_plot)

# Step 2: Sensitivity analysis with expanded covariate set

cat("\n" %+% "=" %>% strrep(70), "\n")
cat("SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS 2: EXPANDED COVARIATE SET\n")
cat("=" %>% strrep(70), "\n\n")

cat("Testing whether including child health status (potential mediator/confounder)\n")
cat("changes the treatment effect estimate.\n\n")

cat("Main adjustment set (", length(x_vars_main), " covariates):\n", sep = "")
cat("  -", paste(x_vars_main, collapse = "\n  - "), "\n\n")
cat("Expanded adjustment set (", length(x_vars_sens), " covariates):\n", sep = "")
cat("  -", paste(x_vars_sens, collapse = "\n  - "), "\n\n")

# Prepare data for sensitivity analysis with expanded covariates
dml_df_sens <- analysis_df %>%
  select(all_of(c(outcome_binary_var, treat_var, x_vars_sens))) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.factor), as.numeric)) %>%
  rename(
    Y = all_of(outcome_binary_var),
    D = all_of(treat_var)
  ) %>%
  drop_na()

cat("Sample size (expanded covariates):", nrow(dml_df_sens), "\n\n")

# Create DoubleML data object
dml_data_sens <- DoubleMLData$new(
  data = dml_df_sens,
  y_col = "Y",
  d_cols = "D",
  x_cols = x_vars_sens
)

# Fit model with expanded covariates
cat("Fitting DML model with expanded covariate set...\n")

ml_g_sens <- lrn("regr.ranger", num.trees = 500, min.node.size = 5)
ml_m_sens <- lrn("classif.ranger", num.trees = 500, min.node.size = 5, 
                 predict_type = "prob")

dml_irm_sens <- DoubleMLIRM$new(
  data = dml_data_sens,
  ml_g = ml_g_sens,
  ml_m = ml_m_sens,
  n_folds = 5,
  n_rep = 1,
  score = "ATE"
)

dml_irm_sens$fit(store_predictions = TRUE)

cat("Model fitted successfully.\n\n")

# Extract results
sens_summary <- dml_irm_sens$summary()

expanded_covar_results <- tibble(
  Model = c("Main Adjustment Set", "Expanded (+ Child Health)"),
  Estimate = c(dml_irm_bin$coef[1], dml_irm_sens$coef[1]),
  SE = c(dml_irm_bin$se[1], dml_irm_sens$se[1]),
  CI_Lower = c(dml_irm_bin$confint()[1, 1], dml_irm_sens$confint()[1, 1]),
  CI_Upper = c(dml_irm_bin$confint()[1, 2], dml_irm_sens$confint()[1, 2]),
  P_Value = c(main_bin_summary$pval[1], sens_summary$pval[1]),
  N_Covariates = c(length(x_vars_main), length(x_vars_sens))
)

cat("Results:\n")
print(expanded_covar_results)

# Calculate percentage change
pct_change <- ((expanded_covar_results$Estimate[2] - expanded_covar_results$Estimate[1]) / 
               abs(expanded_covar_results$Estimate[1])) * 100

cat("\nPercentage change in ATE when adding child health status: ", 
    round(pct_change, 1), "%\n", sep = "")

if (abs(pct_change) < 10) {
  cat("Interpretation: ✓ Results are ROBUST to expanded covariate set\n")
  cat("                 (< 10% change in estimate)\n")
} else if (abs(pct_change) < 25) {
  cat("Interpretation: ⚠ Moderate sensitivity to expanded covariate set\n")
  cat("                 (", round(pct_change, 1), "% change in estimate)\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat("Interpretation: ✗ Results are NOT ROBUST to expanded covariate set\n")
  cat("                 (", round(pct_change, 1), "% change in estimate)\n", sep = "")
}

cat("\n")

# Visualization: Expanded covariates
expanded_covar_plot <- expanded_covar_results %>%
  mutate(Model = factor(Model, levels = Model)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Model, y = Estimate)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = CI_Lower, ymax = CI_Upper),
                width = 0.2, size = 1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(

    subtitle = "Does including child health status change the effect estimate?",
    y = "Average Treatment Effect (ATE)",
    x = "Model Specification",
    caption = paste("Percentage change:", round(pct_change, 1), "%")
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray40"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "gray90")
  )

print(expanded_covar_plot)

# Step 3: Common support trimming (positivity assessment)

cat("\n" %+% "=" %>% strrep(70), "\n")
cat("SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS 3: COMMON SUPPORT TRIMMING\n")
cat("=" %>% strrep(70), "\n\n")

cat("Testing whether results hold when restricting to region of common support.\n")
cat("Common support = propensity score between 0.01 and 0.99\n\n")

# Get propensity scores from binary outcome model
ps_pred_main <- dml_irm_bin$predictions$ml_m

# Check overlap before trimming
poor_overlap_before <- sum(ps_pred_main < 0.01 | ps_pred_main > 0.99)
total_before <- length(ps_pred_main)

cat("Before trimming:\n")
cat("  Total observations:", total_before, "\n")
cat("  Observations in poor overlap region (PS < 0.01 or > 0.99):", poor_overlap_before, "\n")
cat("  Percentage in poor overlap:", round(100 * poor_overlap_before / total_before, 2), "%\n\n")

# Create trimmed dataset (common support region)
dml_df_trim <- dml_df_bin %>%
  mutate(ps = ps_pred_main) %>%
  filter(ps >= 0.01 & ps <= 0.99) %>%
  select(-ps)

cat("After trimming to common support:\n")
cat("  Observations retained:", nrow(dml_df_trim), "\n")
cat("  Observations removed:", total_before - nrow(dml_df_trim), "\n")
cat("  Percentage retained:", round(100 * nrow(dml_df_trim) / total_before, 2), "%\n\n")

# Check treatment balance in trimmed sample
cat("Treatment distribution:\n")
cat("  Before trimming - Treated: ", sum(dml_df_bin$D == 1), " (",
    round(100 * mean(dml_df_bin$D), 2), "%)\n", sep = "")
cat("  After trimming - Treated:  ", sum(dml_df_trim$D == 1), " (",
    round(100 * mean(dml_df_trim$D), 2), "%)\n\n", sep = "")

# Fit model on trimmed sample

  data = dml_df_trim,
  y_col = "Y",
  d_cols = "D",
  x_cols = x_vars_main
)

cat("Fitting DML model on trimmed sample...\n")

dml_irm_trim <- DoubleMLIRM$new(
  data = trim_data,
  ml_g = ml_g_bin,
  ml_m = ml_m_bin,
  n_folds = 5,
  n_rep = 1,
  score = "ATE"
)

dml_irm_trim$fit()

cat("Model fitted successfully.\n\n")

# Extract results
trim_summary <- dml_irm_trim$summary()

common_support_results <- tibble(
  Sample = c("Full Sample", "Common Support Region"),
  N = c(nrow(dml_df_bin), nrow(dml_df_trim)),
  Estimate = c(dml_irm_bin$coef[1], dml_irm_trim$coef[1]),
  SE = c(dml_irm_bin$se[1], dml_irm_trim$se[1]),
  CI_Lower = c(dml_irm_bin$confint()[1, 1], dml_irm_trim$confint()[1, 1]),
  CI_Upper = c(dml_irm_bin$confint()[1, 2], dml_irm_trim$confint()[1, 2]),
  P_Value = c(main_bin_summary$pval[1], trim_summary$pval[1])
)

cat("Results:\n")
print(common_support_results)

# Calculate percentage change
pct_change_trim <- ((common_support_results$Estimate[2] - common_support_results$Estimate[1]) / 
                     abs(common_support_results$Estimate[1])) * 100

cat("\nPercentage change in ATE after common support trimming: ", 
    round(pct_change_trim, 1), "%\n", sep = "")

if (abs(pct_change_trim) < 10) {
  cat("Interpretation: ✓ Results are ROBUST to common support restriction\n")
  cat("                 (< 10% change in estimate)\n")
} else if (abs(pct_change_trim) < 25) {
  cat("Interpretation: ⚠ Moderate sensitivity to common support restriction\n")
  cat("                 (", round(pct_change_trim, 1), "% change in estimate)\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat("Interpretation: ✗ Results are NOT ROBUST to common support restriction\n")
  cat("                 (", round(pct_change_trim, 1), "% change in estimate)\n", sep = "")
}

cat("\n")

# Visualization: Common support

  mutate(Sample = factor(Sample, levels = Sample)) %>%

                width = 0.2, size = 1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(
    title = "Sensitivity Analysis 3: Common Support Trimming",
    subtitle = "Robustness when restricting to region of overlap (PS: 0.01-0.99)",
    y = "Average Treatment Effect (ATE)",

                    "observations removed")
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray40"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "gray90")
  )

print(common_support_plot)

# Step 4: Machine learner sensitivity

cat("Testing whether results are robust to choice of machine learning algorithm.\n")

# Fit model with XGBoost learners
```
