```{r, eval=TRUE}
ml_g_xgb <- lrn("regr.xgboost", nrounds = 100, eta = 0.1, max_depth = 5, verbose = 0)
ml_m_xgb <- lrn("classif.xgboost", nrounds = 100, eta = 0.1, max_depth = 5,
                predict_type = "prob", verbose = 0)

dml_irm_xgb <- DoubleMLIRM$new(
  data = dml_data_bin,
  ml_g = ml_g_xgb,
  ml_m = ml_m_xgb,
  n_folds = 5,
  n_rep = 1,
  score = "ATE"
)

dml_irm_xgb$fit()

cat("XGBoost model fitted successfully.\n\n")

# Extract results
xgb_summary <- dml_irm_xgb$summary()

ml_comparison <- tibble(
  Algorithm = c("Random Forest (Ranger)", "Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)"),
  Estimate = c(dml_irm_bin$coef[1], dml_irm_xgb$coef[1]),
  SE = c(dml_irm_bin$se[1], dml_irm_xgb$se[1]),
  CI_Lower = c(dml_irm_bin$confint()[1, 1], dml_irm_xgb$confint()[1, 1]),
  CI_Upper = c(dml_irm_bin$confint()[1, 2], dml_irm_xgb$confint()[1, 2]),
  P_Value = c(main_bin_summary$pval[1], xgb_summary$pval[1])
)

cat("Results:\n")
print(ml_comparison)

pct_change_ml <- ((ml_comparison$Estimate[2] - ml_comparison$Estimate[1]) / 
                   abs(ml_comparison$Estimate[1])) * 100

cat("\nPercentage change in ATE with different ML algorithm: ", 
    round(pct_change_ml, 1), "%\n", sep = "")

if (abs(pct_change_ml) < 10) {
  cat("Interpretation: ✓ Results are ROBUST to choice of ML algorithm\n")
  cat("                 (< 10% change in estimate)\n")
} else if (abs(pct_change_ml) < 25) {
  cat("Interpretation: ⚠ Moderate sensitivity to ML algorithm choice\n")
  cat("                 (", round(pct_change_ml, 1), "% change in estimate)\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat("Interpretation: ✗ Results are sensitive to ML algorithm choice\n")
  cat("                 (", round(pct_change_ml, 1), "% change in estimate)\n", sep = "")
}

cat("\n")

# Visualization: Machine learner comparison
ml_comp_plot <- ml_comparison %>%
  mutate(Algorithm = factor(Algorithm, levels = Algorithm)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Algorithm, y = Estimate)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = CI_Lower, ymax = CI_Upper),
                width = 0.2, size = 1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(
    title = "Sensitivity Analysis 4: Machine Learner Choice",
    subtitle = "Robustness across Random Forest vs. XGBoost",
    y = "Average Treatment Effect (ATE)",
    x = "Machine Learning Algorithm"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray40"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "gray90")
  )

print(ml_comp_plot)

# Step 5: Master sensitivity table

cat("\n" %+% "=" %>% strrep(70), "\n")
cat("SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS SUMMARY TABLE\n")
cat("=" %>% strrep(70), "\n\n")

sensitivity_summary <- tibble(
  Analysis = c(
    "Main Binary Analysis",
    "Ordinal Outcome",
    "Expanded Covariates",
    "Common Support Trimmed",
    "XGBoost Learners"
  ),
  Estimate = c(
    dml_irm_bin$coef[1],
    dml_plr_ord$coef[1],
    dml_irm_sens$coef[1],
    dml_irm_trim$coef[1],
    dml_irm_xgb$coef[1]
  ),
  SE = c(
    dml_irm_bin$se[1],
    dml_plr_ord$se[1],
    dml_irm_sens$se[1],
    dml_irm_trim$se[1],
    dml_irm_xgb$se[1]
  ),
  P_Value = c(
    main_bin_summary$pval[1],
    main_ord_summary$pval[1],
    sens_summary$pval[1],
    trim_summary$pval[1],
    xgb_summary$pval[1]
  ),
  Significant = c(
    ifelse(main_bin_summary$pval[1] < 0.05, "Yes", "No"),
    ifelse(main_ord_summary$pval[1] < 0.05, "Yes", "No"),
    ifelse(sens_summary$pval[1] < 0.05, "Yes", "No"),
    ifelse(trim_summary$pval[1] < 0.05, "Yes", "No"),
    ifelse(xgb_summary$pval[1] < 0.05, "Yes", "No")
  )
) %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(Estimate, SE, P_Value), ~round(., 6))
  )

print(sensitivity_summary)

# Step 6: Create comprehensive sensitivity plot

cat("\n\nCOMPREHENSIVE SENSITIVITY FOREST PLOT\n")
cat("=" %>% strrep(70), "\n\n")

sensitivity_plot <- sensitivity_summary %>%
  mutate(
    Analysis = factor(Analysis, levels = rev(Analysis)),
    Color = ifelse(Significant == "Yes", "Significant", "Not Significant")
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Analysis, y = Estimate, color = Color)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = Estimate - 1.96*SE, ymax = Estimate + 1.96*SE),
                width = 0.15, size = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Significant" = "darkgreen", "Not Significant" = "gray50")) +
  labs(
    title = "Comprehensive Sensitivity Analysis",
    subtitle = "Robustness of main treatment effect across alternative specifications",
    y = "Average Treatment Effect (ATE)",
    x = "Analysis Specification",
    color = "Significance\n(α = 0.05)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray40"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "gray90")
  ) +
  coord_flip()

print(sensitivity_plot)

# Step 7: Overall robustness assessment

cat("\n\nOVERALL ROBUSTNESS ASSESSMENT\n")
cat("=" %>% strrep(70), "\n\n")

n_specs <- nrow(sensitivity_summary)
n_sig <- sum(sensitivity_summary$Significant == "Yes")

cat("Summary of sensitivity analyses:\n")
cat("  Total alternative specifications tested: ", n_specs, "\n", sep = "")
cat("  Specifications showing significant effects: ", n_sig, "\n", sep = "")
cat("  Percentage consistent with main finding: ", round(100 * n_sig / n_specs, 1), "%\n\n", sep = "")

if (n_sig == n_specs) {
  cat("ROBUSTNESS VERDICT: ✓✓✓ HIGHLY ROBUST\n")
  cat("All alternative specifications support the main finding.\n")
} else if (n_sig >= n_specs * 0.75) {
  cat("ROBUSTNESS VERDICT: ✓✓ MODERATELY ROBUST\n")
  cat("Most alternative specifications support the main finding.\n")
} else if (n_sig >= n_specs * 0.50) {
  cat("ROBUSTNESS VERDICT: ✓ PARTIALLY ROBUST\n")
  cat("About half of alternative specifications support the main finding.\n")
} else {
  cat("ROBUSTNESS VERDICT: ✗ NOT ROBUST\n")
  cat("Few alternative specifications support the main finding.\n")
}

cat("\nKey sensitivity analyses conducted:\n")
cat("  1. Outcome specification (binary vs. ordinal)\n")
cat("  2. Covariate adjustment set (main vs. expanded)\n")
cat("  3. Sample restrictions (full vs. common support region)\n")
cat("  4. Machine learning algorithm (Random Forest vs. XGBoost)\n\n")

cat("========== END OF SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS SECTION ==========\n\n")

```

## Limitations

The findings of this analysis should be interpreted within the context of several limitations, particularly regarding the assumptions required for causal inference.

First, the use of cross-sectional observational data limits the ability to establish temporal ordering between maternal MH and pediatric ED utilization. Although this study conceptualizes maternal MH as the exposure, it is possible that increased child healthcare needs on frequent ED visits may contribute to deteriorated maternal MH, introducing possible reverse causality.

Next, the identification strategy relies on the assumption of no unmeasured confounding. While this study adjusts for a robust set of covariates, unobserved (i.e., uncollected) variables, such as maternal history of trauma, family social support, or neighborhood-level characteristics, may influence both maternal MH and pediatric ED utilization. This could lead to estimated effects that remain biased.

Third, measurement error is a minor, but not insurmountable concern, as all variables in the NSCH are based on caregiver self-report. Maternal MH and child utilization may be subject to recall bias or social desirability bias, which could affect the accuracy of exposure or outcome measurement. Furthermore, child ED utilization is that of a randomly selected child in the household, rather than all children. Therefore, these measures may not fully capture family-level patterns of healthcare use, which could lead to misclassification or attenuation of estimated effects.

Fourth, the relatively small proportion of mothers reporting Fair/Poor MH in the sample may limit statistical power and reduce overlap between treatment groups. This could potentially affect the precision and stability of estimated treatment effects, specifically in the subgroup analyses. A related, but distinct limitation is that the analytic sample is restricted to complete cases, which may introduce selection bias if missingness is systematically related to either maternal MH or child healthcare utilization. This could result in limitations to the generalizability of findings.

Finally, while DML provides a flexible and robust approach to adjusting for observed confounding, its ability to support causal interpretations is conditional on the aforementioned assumptions—all of which have threats.
